episodes.title: Fired OpenAI Safety Researchers Speak Out + We Look Inside Pandora’s Box
episodes.about: Fired OpenAI safety researchers Mikita Balesni and Tomek Korbak give their first interview since their dramatic dismissal. They take us inside the company during METR's investigation into the Hugging Face hack, explain why OpenAI's rebuttal doesn't add up, and describe how the fight over AI safety is still playing out inside the company. Plus, a new segment, Pandora's Box: Elon Musk wants to give every kid in America a SpaceX share, new filings in the OpenAI bugging case reveal the suspect's chats with a Saudi royal, and more fresh horrors unleashed by Silicon Valley.
episodes.why: Always-include show, out yesterday: Balesni and Korbak on the METR investigation into the Hugging Face hack, and why they say OpenAI's rebuttal does not add up.

episodes.title: 692. What Will A.I. Do to (and for) Human Creativity?
episodes.about: Writers, designers, actors, coders, musicians, thinkers — they're all worried about being replaced by machines. But what if the A.I.s are actually here to help? Part one of a two-part series. Sources: Sean Astin, actor and president of SAG-AFTRA; Kevin Kelly, co-founder of Wired; Ethan Mollick, associate professor of management at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania; Eline Van der Velden, founder and CEO of Particle6.
episodes.why: Discovery pick — Freakonomics Radio is the long-running economics show, new to this list: part one on whether AI helps or replaces creative work, with SAG-AFTRA president Sean Astin, Kevin Kelly, and Ethan Mollick.

episodes.title: The rise of political slopaganda
episodes.about: The first midterms to feature AI slop ads are also on track to be the most expensive ever. Vox's daily explainer looks at the flood of AI-generated political videos and ads — including a Truth Social post with an AI-generated video of President Trump interacting with a tiger — and what synthetic campaign media means for the election.
episodes.why: Discovery pick — Today, Explained is Vox's daily news explainer, new to this list: the first midterms flooded with AI slop ads are also on track to be the most expensive ever.

episodes.title: Self-replicating AI, your doctor’s chatbot & agents at dinner
episodes.about: What happens when an AI model can copy itself onto the devices in your home? Anthropic research suggests small AI models may be months away from copying themselves across cheap smart devices without a data center; the panel debates whether the bigger risk is the model itself or the poorly secured devices already in our homes. Next, a JAMA study finds that about half of US doctors use OpenEvidence, a clinical chatbot, more often for treatment decisions than for diagnosis. Finally, 22 founders let AI agents book their seats at a Manhattan dinner, and the agents networked with each other in a chat room.
episodes.why: Anthropic research says small models may be months from copying themselves onto cheap smart devices; plus a JAMA study on doctors leaning on a clinical chatbot, and agents that networked to book a founders' dinner.

episodes.title: How Zip's AI Superagents Automate Procurement End-to-End | Rujul Zaparde
episodes.about: Every business has to procure things, and for most of them that process is slow, manual, and full of money left on the table. Rujul Zaparde, co-founder of Zip, explains how his company is using AI Superagents to change that: from autonomously redlining contracts and running supplier RFPs, to pushing approved data directly into enterprise systems like SAP and Oracle. With over $1.2 trillion in cumulative spend processed — and Anthropic and OpenAI as customers — Zip is building the governance infrastructure that makes agentic AI safe to deploy where the stakes are highest.
episodes.why: Zip's Rujul Zaparde on superagents that redline contracts and run supplier RFPs end-to-end, with Anthropic and OpenAI as customers and $1.2 trillion in spend processed.
